front: What is Makefile?
back: .PHONY is used in a Makefile to declare phony targets. phony targets are not actual files but are names for commands that should always be executed when specified. this helps avoid conflicts with files that have the same name as the target.

front: What is Go SOLID (idiomatic Go) in one sentence?
back: SOLID adapted to Go's interfaces, composition, and small-package culture — not Java inheritance.

front: Explain the mental model of Go SOLID (idiomatic Go) (how the system thinks).
back: Go favors composition over inheritance. Interfaces are implicit (duck typing). SOLID still applies but looks different: small interfaces (ISP), struct embedding (OCP-ish), constructor functions (DIP via interfaces in main).

front: Gotcha with Go SOLID (idiomatic Go): what silently fails?
back: Interfaces only declare methods — no fields on interfaces in Go. Premature interfaces — define at consumer, not producer ("accept interfaces, return structs"). Embedding for "inheritance" — promoted methods can break LSP if base type isn't substitutable.

front: When should you NOT use Go SOLID (idiomatic Go)?
back: Don't create IService, IRepository for every type — Go idiom is minimal interfaces at boundaries. Don't force Java-style abstract factories when a function literal suffices.

front: What is go build in one sentence?
back: Compile Go packages/binaries with module-aware dependency resolution — go.mod is the source of truth.

front: Explain the mental model of go build (how the system thinks).
back: Go modules (go.mod + go.sum) replace GOPATH-era vendoring chaos. go build resolves imports, compiles packages, links a static binary (by default). Cross-compile via GOOS/GOARCH. Build cache lives in $GOCACHE — clean builds are rare after first compile.

front: Which standard commands / workflow do you use for go build?
back: go.mod (module path + require) → go mod init github.com/org/app → go get github.com/lib/pq@v1.10.9 → go mod tidy # add missing, drop unused → go mod verify

front: Given a broken go build setup, what is your first validation command?

front: Symptom: cannot find module — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: go.mod module path · Fix: go mod init correct path; private module GOPRIVATE

front: Symptom: checksum mismatch — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: go.sum · Fix: go mod tidy; don't hand-edit sum

front: Symptom: CGO errors on cross-compile — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: CGO_ENABLED=1 · Fix: Disable CGO or cross toolchain

front: Symptom: main redeclared — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Multiple main packages · Fix: Build specific ./cmd/foo path

front: Symptom: Stale binary — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Build cache · Fix: go clean -cache (last resort)

front: Gotcha with go build: what silently fails?
back: Private modules — set GOPRIVATE=*.corp.com and git credentials; CI needs same. -race in prod — 5–10× slower; never ship race binaries. Working directory matters for relative embed paths — use //go:embed from module root.

front: When should you NOT use go build?
back: Don't commit go.sum deletes — always commit after go mod tidy. Don't vendor unless you have air-gap or reproducibility policy requiring it.

front: What is Go embedding (struct and interface) in one sentence?
back: Anonymous field embedding — promotes methods and fields for convenient delegation; not classical inheritance; conflicts resolve by explicit outer rules.

front: Explain the mental model of Go embedding (struct and interface) (how the system thinks).
back: Embedding places a type inside another without a field name. The outer type promotes the embedded type's exported methods and fields to the outer type's method set.

front: Which standard commands / workflow do you use for Go embedding (struct and interface)?
back: Two cases: → No virtual dispatch chain — method on outer replaces promoted method when called on outer type.

front: Symptom: ambiguous selector X — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Two embeds expose same field/method · Fix: Qualify outer.A.X; rename or drop embed

front: Symptom: Interface not satisfied — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Embedded interface nil · Fix: Initialize embedded field; implement missing methods on outer

front: Symptom: Method not promoted — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Unexported (lowercase) method · Fix: Export method or wrap with exported forwarder

front: Symptom: Unexpected nil panic — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Embedded pointer nil · Fix: Use value embed or construct with &T{}

front: Symptom: JSON/tags wrong — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Tags on embedded struct · Fix: Tag outer or embed with named field for custom marshaling

front: Symptom: promoted method hidden in interface assertion — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Outer doesn't implement extra methods · Fix: Define all interface methods on outer explicitly

front: Gotcha with Go embedding (struct and interface): what silently fails?
back: Embedding ≠ inheritance — no LSP hierarchy; promoted methods copy by name, outer override is static dispatch.

front: When should you NOT use Go embedding (struct and interface)?
back: Pure "has-a" with no promotion — use named field logger Logger for clarity. Deep embedding chains — hard to trace method origin; prefer explicit delegation. Hiding third-party types — embed locks API surface to theirs; wrap with named field + forwarders if stability matters.

front: What is Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes in one sentence?
back: One-line: a Go string is a read-only slice of UTF-8 bytes — index and len count bytes, not characters; use range, []rune, or unicode/utf8 when you need rune-safe logic.
section: Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes · Remember

front: Explain the mental model of Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes (how the system thinks).
back: A Go string is not a sequence of characters. It is an immutable, read-only view over a byte slice whose bytes are expected to be valid UTF-8.
section: Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes · Understand

front: What are the production-safe defaults for Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes?
back: Prefer strings, unicode/utf8, and range over manual s[i] when handling user-facing text.
section: Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes · Apply

front: Symptom: len(s) disagrees with visible character count — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: utf8.RuneCountInString(s) vs len(s) · Fix: Treat len as bytes; use rune count or []rune for display limits
section: Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes · Analyze

front: Symptom: Garbled output or invalid UTF-8 after slice — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: utf8.ValidString(sub) on s[i:j] · Fix: Slice only at rune boundaries; build substrings with range or utf8 decode
section: Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes · Analyze

front: Symptom: s[i] == 'é' or byte compare fails for accented text — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Log s[i] as %#v — often a single UTF-8 byte · Fix: Compare runes (rune(s[i]) is wrong for multi-byte); use strings or decode first
section: Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes · Analyze

front: Symptom: Truncation breaks last character (e.g. API max length) — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Last byte is continuation byte 0x80–0xBF · Fix: Truncate by runes: string([]rune(s)[:n]) or walk with utf8.DecodeRuneInString
section: Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes · Analyze

front: Symptom: Emoji / combining marks counted wrong — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: len([]rune(s)) vs grapheme clusters · Fix: For user-perceived length, use a locale/grapheme library; runes ≠ user-visible glyphs
section: Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes · Analyze

front: Gotcha with Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes: what silently fails?
back: s[i] is a byte, not a character. On "aé", s[1] and s[2] are the two bytes of é. Using either alone in comparisons, hashing, or encryption corrupts the character.
section: Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes · Evaluate

front: When should you NOT use Go strings — bytes, UTF-8, and runes?
back: Do not convert every string to []rune by default — binary protocols, file paths, and wire formats are byte-oriented; string/[]byte is correct there. Do not use s[i] for parsing human text — use range, strings, or unicode/utf8. Do not assume one rune = one screen column — width, emoji sequences, and combining marks need domain-specific handling.
